title: Why Scrapers Still Hit HTTP 429 Errors Despite Delays
summary: Adding delays isn't enough. Fix HTTP 429 errors by tackling fingerprint inconsistency, session leakage, and rate-bucket…
body_markdown:
Adding delays between scraper requests often fails to prevent HTTP 429 errors. Servers enforce rate limits by *identity signals* (browser fingerprints, session tokens and concurrent request patterns), not just by request timing. The fix is to find which identity the server is counting and pace that identity, not just the clock.


## Key takeaways


- HTTP 429 errors persist despite delays because servers group requests by fingerprint (user-agent, TLS cipher, screen resolution) and session state, not just timestamps.
- Rate-limit algorithms like token buckets and sliding windows count requests *per identifier* (IP address, session token, fingerprint hash), so timing changes alone rarely help.
- Rotating proxies while the fingerprint stays the same doesn't split the identity: servers see many IPs sharing one fingerprint hash and keep returning 429.
- Session cookies and localStorage persist across proxy rotations unless explicitly cleared, so the server keeps grouping requests under one identity.
- Infrastructure that keeps fingerprints consistent within a session and clears state between sessions removes most avoidable 429s without manual session management.


## Why HTTP 429 errors happen even with request delays


Adding delays between requests fixes *timing* but not *identity* . Servers count requests in a window, often a sliding window over the last N seconds, but they group those requests by identifier: IP address, session token, TLS signature or browser attributes. When your scraper's identity signals cluster together, the server sees one persistent actor making many requests, even if those requests arrive seconds apart. Three hidden causes drive this clustering. Fingerprint inconsistency: requests expose User-Agent or header combinations no real browser would send, which flags the traffic as automated. Session-state leakage: cookies or tokens from one request carry into the next and link them. Concurrent bursts: parallel threads share one IP or credential, so their delays collapse into simultaneous hits.


### What HTTP 429 Too Many Requests really means


[HTTP 429 Too Many Requests](https://zuplo.com/learning-center/http-429-too-many-requests-guide) is the server's signal that a client exceeded the allowed request rate within a time window. Websites rate-limit to protect server resources and curb abusive automation. Two models dominate: token buckets hand out a fixed number of request tokens that refill at a steady rate, while sliding windows count requests over a rolling period instead of fixed minute boundaries. When your identifier (IP address, API key or session token) exhausts its quota, the server rejects further requests with a 429, often with a Retry-After header saying when to try again.


### The delay fallacy: timing vs identity


Slowing your request rate assumes the server counts only timestamps. Production rate limiters count requests *per identifier* , not per second. If your scraper sends ten requests over sixty seconds and all ten share one IP address and one TLS fingerprint, they land in a single bucket. The delay spreads the timeline but doesn't split the identity. Fingerprint-aware systems track User-Agent consistency, header order, cipher suite negotiation and session continuity, so adding sleep calls between identical requests changes little. That's why scrapers that rotate proxies but reuse session cookies, or vary User-Agent strings but keep identical Accept-Language headers, keep hitting 429 errors despite respecting timing intervals.[Anakin's infrastructure](https://anakin.io/blog/cloudflare-blocking-automation-system-fix) handles this pairing for you: the URL Scraper routes requests through residential proxies in 207 countries and territories, and useBrowser sends them through a managed, fingerprint-masked browser, so a request's network and browser signals agree with each other.

## How server-side rate limiting actually works


Client-side delays address only half the problem. The server doesn't see the pauses between requests; it sees arrival timestamps and identity clusters. Most production systems layer several buckets, each tracking a different dimension of identity.


### Sliding window vs token bucket algorithms


Rate-limit enforcement typically uses one of two models. A sliding window algorithm counts requests within the last N seconds and rejects once the threshold is reached. Anakin's own API works this way, per its[rate limits docs](https://anakin.io/docs/documentation/rate-limits) : 60 requests per minute for most submit endpoints such as POST /v1/url-scraper, 10 per minute for AI evaluation, and no limit on URL Scraper and Search polling (GET /v1/url-scraper/{id}). Each endpoint is an independent bucket. The window slides continuously, so a burst at second 58 and another at second 2 of the next minute both count inside the same 60-second span.


A token bucket refills capacity at a fixed rate, five tokens per second for example. A burst consumes tokens instantly; when the bucket is empty, requests wait for the refill. This model permits short bursts but enforces a sustained average. The choice changes retry behavior: sliding windows reward spreading requests across the full period, while token buckets tolerate short bursts followed by pauses.


### Per-IP vs per-session vs per-fingerprint limits


Modern servers can enforce rate limits across three independent identity layers:


1. **Per-IP bucket** is the coarsest signal. Traffic spread across many addresses keeps each IP's count low, but a single residential proxy shared by many users hits the limit quickly.
2. **Per-session bucket** is keyed by cookies or session tokens. Rotating proxies doesn't clear this counter if the session persists across IP changes. Dropping cookies after every request avoids building a session count, but it also gives up any logged-in state the scrape depends on.
3. **Per-fingerprint bucket** groups requests into recognizable cohorts by TLS handshake patterns and HTTP/2 frame order, even when IP and session change. A default headless Puppeteer setup shares its fingerprint with many other Puppeteer instances, so one abusive actor can exhaust the bucket for the whole cohort.


Changing one dimension (switching proxies, clearing cookies or swapping user-agent strings) doesn't reset the others. The server tracks all three in parallel, and whichever bucket fills first returns the 429. So identity clustering can trip a limit long before your overall request rate gets near it.


## Three hidden causes of persistent 429 errors


Most scraping guides prescribe delays and proxy rotation as the universal 429 fix. When those fail, the root cause usually isn't volume. It's identity signals that group requests under one automated fingerprint even as IPs rotate.


### Browser fingerprint inconsistency across requests


Anti-bot systems probe browser artifacts to spot automation: user-agent strings, screen resolution, timezone, installed fonts, WebGL renderer and TLS cipher-suite order. When a scraper rotates proxies but sends the same fingerprint profile, or sends attribute combinations no real browser would produce, the server groups those requests into one automated cluster and applies limits at the cluster level. The[FP-Inconsistent study (ACM IMC 2025)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3730567.3732919) sent half a million requests from 20 commercial bot services to a honey site protected by DataDome and BotD. The bots evaded detection 52.93% and 44.56% of the time, but their fingerprints were often internally inconsistent, and rules built on those inconsistencies cut evasion by roughly 45 to 48%.


Servers can hash request characteristics (user-agent string, TLS cipher suite, screen resolution, timezone, installed fonts, WebGL renderer) into a fingerprint that survives IP changes. If browser attributes don't change along with the proxy, the hash stays constant. Behavior counts too:[research on fingerprinting AI browsing agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01247) found that typing, scrolling and mouse patterns separated seven AI agents from humans and from each other, even where their browser fingerprints were shared.


That's the proxy rotation trap. Many IPs sharing one fingerprint hash is a pattern typical of bot infrastructure, and when the limiter buckets by fingerprint rather than IP, each new proxy connection adds to the same counter. Once the per-fingerprint threshold trips, the server returns 429 across every IP tied to that hash, and the rotation buys nothing.


### Session state leakage (cookies and localStorage persistence)


Rotating IPs does not clear cookies or localStorage unless the scraper manages the session lifecycle. When a request carries a session token or tracking cookie from a previous IP's session, the server links the new IP to the old identity and applies the cumulative count. The[FP-Inconsistent study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07647) also checked consistency across time (the same attribute observed at two points), which is exactly the comparison that carried-over state makes possible.


Cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB all outlive proxy rotation, and anti-bot systems read them to recognize returning clients after the IP changes.


Session cookies carrying JWTs or authentication state stay in the scraper's context across proxy hops unless explicitly dropped, and a single login cookie can bind hundreds of requests to one identity. When a 403 or 429 points to a flagged session, clear its cookies before retrying so the next request doesn't inherit it.


Headless browser scrapers also inherit localStorage and IndexedDB entries from prior runs: device IDs, feature flags, interaction timestamps. Proxy rotation alone doesn't clear them, so each new IP carries the same client-side footprint until the browser context is torn down.


Three session-lifecycle steps limit the leakage:


1. Clear cookies and storage before each proxy rotation to drop inherited session artifacts.
2. Isolate browser contexts using separate profiles or container tabs so that parallel requests do not share state.
3. Validate session expiry before retrying, so a flagged credential isn't reused after a failed request.


### Concurrent request clustering and batch patterns


Servers also detect batch patterns when request timing clusters, even with random jitter added. A[2026 bot-detection measurement study](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.14525v1) summarizes earlier work that crawled the Alexa Top 10K with headless Chromium: of 291 sites that blocked the crawler, 93 (about a third) used browser fingerprinting rather than simple per-IP thresholds. When several requests from one identity (fingerprint plus session) arrive in a narrow window, batch heuristics fire regardless of per-request delays. Cap concurrency per identity and keep sessions isolated, rather than relying on spacing alone.


## Diagnose which bucket you're hitting


A 429 can be tied to different identities: IP address, session, account, API key, cookie or client fingerprint. Work through these checks in order:


1. Check for a Retry-After header. If it's present, honor it: Retry-After: 120 means wait 120 seconds.
2. Test whether changing the IP alone stops the 429s. If it does, the limit is per-IP, and each IP needs pacing under it.
3. If not, compare fingerprints across your requests: TLS signature, user-agent, header order. Inconsistent or default headless values point to a per-fingerprint bucket.
4. If 429s continue, check session state. The limit may be tied to cookies or localStorage carried between requests.


## Reading and acting on Retry-After headers


When a server returns HTTP 429, it often includes a Retry-After header saying how long to wait. Scrapers that ignore it and retry immediately trigger more 429s and compound the problem. Retry logic that parses and honors Retry-After breaks that loop.


### Parsing Retry-After header values


The *Retry-After* header ships in two formats: delay-seconds (integer, e.g. *120* ) or an HTTP-date (absolute timestamp, e.g. *Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT* ). Robust scrapers must handle both. Try parsing as an integer first, then fall back to an HTTP-date parser. Then add a little random jitter on top of the wait (10 to 15% works) so parallel workers don't all retry at the same instant.


```text
import random
import time
import requests
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from datetime import datetime, timezone


def parse_retry_after(header_value: str) -> float:
# Return seconds to wait, from either a delay-seconds or HTTP-date value.
try:
return max(0.0, float(int(header_value)))
except ValueError:
retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(header_value)
delta = (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
return max(0.0, delta)


def fetch_with_backoff(url: str, max_retries: int = 5):
for attempt in range(max_retries):
r = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
if r.status_code != 429:
return r
header = r.headers.get('Retry-After')
# Honor Retry-After when present; otherwise back off exponentially.
wait = parse_retry_after(header) if header else min(60, 2 ** attempt)
# Add 10-15% jitter on top so parallel workers don't retry in lockstep.
time.sleep(wait * random.uniform(1.10, 1.15))
raise RuntimeError(f'Exhausted retries for {url}')
```


### Exponential backoff implementation


When *Retry-After* is absent, exponential backoff is the standard fallback: start with a short delay and double it on each retry, with random jitter. The[tenacity](https://tenacity.readthedocs.io/) library handles this cleanly, and its wait_random_exponential applies full jitter up to a cap.


```text
import requests
from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential, retry_if_exception_type


class RateLimited(Exception):
pass


@retry(
retry=retry_if_exception_type(RateLimited),
wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=1, max=60),
stop=stop_after_attempt(6),
reraise=True,
)
def scrape(url: str):
r = requests.get(url, timeout=30)
if r.status_code == 429:
raise RateLimited(r.headers.get('Retry-After'))
r.raise_for_status()
return r.json()
```


Backoff alone doesn't help when every retry lands in an identity bucket that's already full. In that case, slow the identity being counted: honor Retry-After, lower concurrency per session or IP, and drop a flagged session's cookies instead of reusing them. ## Pace the identity, not just the clock


Choose exponential backoff when:


- The 429 is infrequent and you have engineering capacity to implement retry logic with jitter.
- Your volume stays well under the published rate limit and you can afford to slow down requests.


Choose an infrastructure service like Anakin when:


- The limit is tied to fingerprint or session state, so IP rotation alone won't fix it.
- You'd rather not build and maintain proxy routing, browser fingerprints and retry orchestration yourself.

## Frequently asked questions


### Why do scrapers still get 429 errors after adding random delays between requests?


Delays address timing, not identity clustering. Servers count requests per fingerprint, IP address, session token or browser signature within a window, not per second. Requests sharing the same fingerprint accumulate in the same bucket, and once it's full, the server returns 429 no matter how they were spaced.


### What's the difference between per-IP and per-session rate limits?


Per-IP limits count requests from one IP address within a time window, regardless of session. Per-session limits count requests from one session cookie or fingerprint hash, regardless of the IP address used. When servers layer both, rotating proxies solves only the per-IP constraint; per-session buckets keep filling until the session state is cleared or the session slows down.


### Does rotating proxies fix HTTP 429 errors?


Not on its own when servers enforce per-fingerprint or per-session buckets. Production rate limiters count requests *per identifier* , not per second. Keep each session's fingerprint consistent, clear session state (cookies, localStorage) between jobs, and pace each identity under its limit.


### How do you parse the Retry-After header in Python?


Check whether *Retry-After* is present in *response.headers* . Parse as an integer (delay-seconds) or as an HTTP-date string with *email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime* . See the *parse_retry_after* helper earlier in this post for a reference implementation.


### What browser fingerprinting signals do servers track?


Common signals include the user-agent string, screen resolution, timezone, installed fonts, WebGL renderer and TLS cipher suite. Hashed together, they form a fingerprint that survives IP changes. Inconsistent or generic fingerprints, such as headless Chrome defaults, expose scrapers even when proxies rotate.


### When does exponential backoff fail to fix 429 errors?


When every retry lands in the same identity bucket. The server sees the retries as the same automated source, so the count keeps climbing whatever the backoff interval. This happens when a scraper keeps reusing a flagged session or keeps sending from one overloaded identity; slowing that identity and clearing the flagged session's state fixes it.
